Action RPG: Role-playing games whose core loop combines real-time action combat with character levels, equipment, skills, or build customization. Turn-based RPGs and action games with only minor upgrades do not qualify.
Atmospheric: Games that place strong emphasis on an immersive mood or sense of place through their environments, visual style, sound, or environmental storytelling. Attractive graphics alone are not enough.
Automation: Games where designing systems that operate with little ongoing manual input is a central mechanic, such as production lines, logistics networks, programmable machines, or automated resource processing. A minor auto-crafting feature alone is not enough.
Building: Games where constructing and customizing structures, bases, settlements, or other creations is a substantial part of play. Includes creative and survival building, but not games where placing an occasional structure is incidental.
Bullet Time: Games with a prominent slow-motion mechanic used during combat to aim, dodge, or plan actions. Cinematic slow-motion cutscenes or ordinary pause menus do not qualify.
City Builder: Games centered on designing, expanding, and maintaining a city or settlement, including infrastructure, services, inhabitants, and resource needs. Building only a personal base is not enough.
Co-op: Games with a supported mode where two or more human players work together toward shared objectives, locally or online. Competitive multiplayer and AI companions alone do not qualify.
FPS: First-person shooters where aiming and firing guns or similar ranged weapons is a central gameplay mechanic. A first-person viewpoint without substantial shooting does not qualify.
Farming Simulator: Games where cultivating crops, raising livestock, or operating and developing a farm is a central gameplay loop. Includes realistic farming simulations and farming-focused life sims, but not games with only optional gardening.
Fast-Paced: Games whose main gameplay regularly demands rapid reactions, movement, or decisions, such as high-speed combat, racing, or action challenges. Occasional timed sections in otherwise slow-paced games are not enough.
Favorites: A personal collection requiring explicit evidence that this library owner has marked the game as a favorite. Do not infer membership from popularity, reviews, quality, genre, or playtime. Without the owner's stated preference, this category does not apply.
Fighting: Fighting games centered on direct character-versus-character bouts using attacks, combos, blocking, spacing, or similar combat techniques. Includes traditional and platform fighters. Generic melee combat in an action game is not enough.
Funny: Games that deliberately make comedy, jokes, absurd situations, parody, or humorous writing a substantial part of the experience. Lighthearted visuals or occasional jokes alone are not enough.
Hidden: A personal collection requiring explicit evidence that this library owner has chosen to hide the game in Steam. Do not infer membership from obscurity, low ratings, mature content, or limited appeal. Without the owner's stated decision, this category does not apply.
Horror: Games designed primarily to create fear, dread, or sustained tension through horror themes, threatening encounters, disturbing imagery, or vulnerability. Dark settings or monsters alone are not enough.
Idler: Idle or incremental games where accumulating resources, buying upgrades, and increasing production rates are central mechanics, with substantial progress occurring automatically or during low-input play. A passive reward system in another genre is not enough.
Local Co-op: Games that support two or more human players cooperating on the same device through shared-screen or split-screen play. Online-only co-op and local competitive modes do not qualify.
Looter Shooter: Shooters whose core loop combines gun combat with repeatedly acquiring weapons or equipment of varying stats, rarity, or effects to improve character builds. Ordinary weapon pickups in a shooter are not enough.
MMORPG: Massively multiplayer online role-playing games with a persistent shared world, many simultaneous players, and ongoing character progression. Small-group online RPGs and ordinary multiplayer matchmaking do not qualify.
Management: Games centered on running and optimizing an organization or system by allocating resources, setting priorities, and balancing constraints. Includes businesses, colonies, parks, hospitals, and similar operations. Managing a character inventory alone is not enough.
Metroidvania: Exploration-focused games with an interconnected map where acquiring movement abilities or tools unlocks previously inaccessible areas and encourages backtracking. Usually combines platforming and combat; a linear platformer with upgrades alone is not enough.
Misc: Games with unusual or experimental core gameplay that does not clearly fit a conventional gameplay genre. Do not use this as a general catch-all for games with an identifiable genre or simply because information is missing.
Multiplayer: Games with a supported mode where multiple human players participate together, cooperatively or competitively, locally or online. Leaderboards, asynchronous score comparisons, or AI opponents alone do not qualify.
Open World: Games with a large, substantially connected world that players can freely explore, with meaningful choice in destinations or activities beyond a fixed sequence of levels. A small hub or isolated sandbox arena alone is not enough.
Platformer: Games where navigating environments by running, jumping, climbing, or traversing platforms is a central mechanic. Occasional jumping in another genre is not enough.
Precision Platformer: Platformers built around demanding, tightly timed jumps and movement sequences, often with small margins for error, frequent retries, and mastery of challenging routes. Ordinary platforming sections alone do not qualify.
Puzzle: Games where solving logical, spatial, mechanical, or deduction-based problems is a central gameplay activity. Occasional puzzles in an otherwise unrelated game are not enough.
RPG: Role-playing games where developing a character or party through meaningful stats, skills, equipment, builds, or role-based choices is central to play. Includes action and turn-based RPGs. A minor upgrade tree alone is not enough.
Racing: Games centered on racing vehicles or other controllable competitors against opponents, a clock, or course records. Driving as transportation in another genre does not qualify.
Relaxing: Games suitable for playing while listening to an audiobook or occasionally looking at a video, with low-pressure, repetitive, self-paced, or readily pausable gameplay. Understanding spoken dialogue, following a dense story, reacting to important audio cues, or maintaining constant precision should not be necessary for the main gameplay loop. A cozy appearance alone is not enough.
Rhythm: Games where timing player actions to music, a beat, or rhythmic patterns is a central mechanic. Having a prominent soundtrack without beat-based interaction does not qualify.
Roguetop: Roguelike and roguelite games built around repeated runs with procedural variation, randomized encounters or rewards, and substantial loss of run progress on failure. Includes games with persistent upgrades between runs and both turn-based and real-time combat.
Simulation: Games centered on modeling real-world or plausible activities, processes, or systems, such as driving, flying, farming, operating machinery, or life simulation. Realistic graphics alone do not qualify.
Singleplayer: Games with a substantial supported mode designed to be played by one human player, including solo campaigns and self-contained solo gameplay. Multiplayer-only games do not qualify merely because a player can queue alone.
Souls-like: Games modeled on Souls-style design, with deliberate and challenging combat, attack commitment, careful dodging or blocking, checkpoint-based exploration, and meaningful consequences for death. Difficulty alone is not enough.
Stealth: Games where avoiding detection, using cover or concealment, planning infiltration, or silently bypassing enemies is a central or substantial supported playstyle. A crouch button or occasional stealth sequence alone is not enough.
Story Rich: Games where a developed narrative, characters, dialogue, or consequential story choices form a major part of the experience. Includes linear and branching stories. Background lore or a minimal premise without substantial narrative content is not enough.
Strategy: Games where tactical or strategic planning, positioning, resource allocation, or coordinated decisions are central to success. Includes real-time and turn-based strategy. Routine combat decisions in an action game alone are not enough.
Survival: Games where gathering resources, crafting tools or shelter, and managing ongoing environmental threats or bodily needs are central to surviving and progressing. Merely staying alive during combat or surviving timed enemy waves is not enough.
Survivor-like: Games resembling Vampire Survivors, with run-based play against large, escalating enemy waves, frequent upgrade choices, collectible experience or resources, and survival for a duration or until a boss objective. Automatic attacks are common but not required. Ordinary survival crafting games or shooters with an incidental horde mode do not qualify.
Utilities: Non-game software such as creation tools, editors, benchmarking programs, desktop utilities, or productivity applications. A game with an integrated editor or crafting tools does not qualify solely for those features.
VR: Games or applications with an officially supported virtual-reality mode or a requirement to use a VR headset. Both VR-only titles and games with an optional VR mode qualify; unofficial mods alone do not.
